system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, orthostatic hypotension, anxiety, and GERD was admitted for acute-onset chest pain radiating to the back, neck, and shoulders, associated with nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and diarrhea. She had recently been evaluated at another hospital and returned due to worsening symptoms. Evaluation revealed no evidence of acute cardiac ischemia, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection on CT angiography, and serial troponins were negative. There were no objective signs of mast cell degranulation, and her symptoms improved without specific intervention. The EpiPen was temporarily withheld due to risk of hypertensive crisis given her history of epinephrine-related MI. Urinalysis showed no infection. She was discharged home asymptomatic on her prior medications with instructions to follow up with her PCP and specialists. She briefly returned to the ED post-discharge due to anxiety but was cleared and discharged again.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with itching, chest tightness, and nausea. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a cold for two days—fever, cough, congestion. Then yesterday, it triggered one of my mast cell attacks. I got intense itching, chest pressure, stomach pain, and started vomiting. I couldn’t take my usual Benadryl at home because I threw it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were given IV Benadryl and Ativan in the ER. The nursing team said you were sleeping between episodes but woke up distressed with itching and chest tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I was so itchy I couldn’t stay still. I asked for Dilaudid too, but they gave me more Benadryl and I felt better after a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re treating this as a flare of your mast cell degranulation syndrome. You’ve had these before, and they can be triggered by infections like this cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been admitted almost monthly lately. Last time, they gave me IV epinephrine and I had heart rhythm problems. I’m scared of that happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Because of your history—especially the MI after a high dose of epinephrine—we’re avoiding epinephrine unless absolutely necessary. We’ll stick to your protocol: Benadryl, Ativan, and oral Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s what usually works. But why does this keep happening so often now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely your immune system is more reactive, especially with your other conditions like rheumatoid arthritis. We’re also reviewing whether you’ve been taking all your preventive meds. I see you haven’t been on montelukast for a month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to refill it. I didn’t think it was that important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may help reduce the frequency of these flares. We’re restarting it today. Also, your allergist notes that past evaluations haven’t shown classic signs of anaphylaxis—no low blood pressure or airway swelling—so we’re balancing treatment with safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the symptoms feel real. The chest tightness, the nausea—it’s terrifying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They absolutely are real to you, and we’re not dismissing that. Even if labs don’t show mast cell activation, your symptoms are valid and we’re treating them. You’re getting IV Benadryl as needed and we’ll transition you to oral as you keep it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. What about my breathing? I felt short of breath last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows only minimal atelectasis—just a small area of collapsed lung tissue, likely from shallow breathing during discomfort. No pneumonia or fluid. Your lungs sound clear now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I always worry about that after the MI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG is normal—normal rhythm, no changes from your last one. We checked a cardiac enzyme once and it was negative. No sign of a heart attack this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad. So this was just the mast cell flare, not something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it appears to be a typical flare, triggered by your upper respiratory infection. We’re monitoring you closely, but you’re already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. The itching is gone, and my chest feels open. I haven’t needed any pain meds since this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re going to switch your Benadryl to oral form so you can take it at home as needed. You’ve been off montelukast for a month—let’s restart it to help prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to take it daily. Should I be worried about the pulmonary nodules they found last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy came back showing organizing pneumonia, not cancer. It’s likely related to inflammation from your immune system. Your rheumatologist and pulmonologist are aware and will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was really scared it was something worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. We’ll make sure you have follow-up appointments. For now, you’re doing well—eating, no vomiting, symptoms resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if you stay stable. Any concerns?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if another flare happens at home? Should I go to the ER right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you have severe symptoms—especially trouble breathing or chest pain—you should go to the ER. But try your oral Benadryl first, and call your allergist. Avoid epinephrine unless instructed—remember your heart risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I should take the montelukast every day, even when I feel fine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s a preventive medication. Also, keep using your nasal cromolyn and fexofenadine—they help control mast cell activity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything. I feel much calmer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve had a quiet night—no symptoms, vitals stable. We’re going to discharge you in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will my medications be the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly yes. We’ve updated your omeprazole to twice daily for better stomach protection, and you’ll now take nitrofurantoin daily and at bedtime for urinary protection. Most importantly, you’re back on montelukast daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Benadryl for itching?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll have 50 mg capsules—take one every six hours as needed. Also keep using Ativan for anxiety if needed, and your rescue inhaler for any breathing tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my PCP and allergist. Should I see anyone else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your rheumatologist and pulmonologist should see you given your RA and the organizing pneumonia finding. We’ll send all the records and set up referrals if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I really appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if symptoms return. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of mast cell degranulation syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and prior epinephrine-induced MI was admitted for a typical mast cell flare triggered by an upper respiratory infection. She presented with itching, chest tightness, epigastric pain, and vomiting, and was treated with IV Benadryl, Ativan, and oral Dilaudid as needed. Her symptoms resolved overnight. A chest X-ray showed only minimal atelectasis with no acute process, and EKG was unchanged without cardiac ischemia. She was restarted on montelukast, which she had not taken for a month, and discharged home with updated medications and follow-up plans. No procedures were performed.
